# Analysis {#sec-analysis}

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.api as sm
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine=create_engine(os.environ["AUTORACK_URL"])
df=pd.read_sql("""
select ca.county_fips, ca.year, ca.affordability_salary,
    cte.routine_cognitive_share, cte.routine_manual_share,
    cte.non_routine_cognitive_share, cte.non_routine_manual_share,
    cb.poverty_rate, cb.unemployment_rate, cb.population
from county_affordability ca
join county_task_exposure cte on ca.county_fips=cte.county_fips and ca.year=cte.year
join county_baseline cb on ca.county_fips=cb.county_fips and ca.year=cb.year
""", engine)
df["log_population"]=np.log(df["population"])
```

```{python}
#| include: false
# level model: OLS with year indicators, standard errors clustered by county
reg_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share",
          "poverty_rate","unemployment_rate","log_population"]

reg=df.dropna(subset=reg_cols+["affordability_salary"]).copy()

X=pd.concat([reg[reg_cols],
             pd.get_dummies(reg["year"], prefix="year", drop_first=True).astype(float)], axis=1)
X=sm.add_constant(X)

model=sm.OLS(reg["affordability_salary"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})

reg.loc[:, "fitted"]=model.fittedvalues
reg.loc[:, "resid"]=model.resid

# log respecification, same design matrix
reg.loc[:, "actual_log"]=np.log(reg["affordability_salary"])
model_log=sm.OLS(reg["actual_log"], X).fit(
    cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": reg["county_fips"]})

reg.loc[:, "fitted_log"]=model_log.fittedvalues
reg.loc[:, "resid_log"]=model_log.resid
```

## What the data look like before modeling

Two features of the data shape every modeling decision that follows.

The first is the shape of the outcome. Purchasing power is right skewed, with a skewness of 1.17. The center sits near \$57,000 and a long tail of high purchasing power counties extends above it. A linear model fits the conditional mean and assumes errors that scatter symmetrically around it, so a skewed outcome carries a standing risk of skewed residuals concentrated in the upper tail.

The second is the spread of the four task groups. Each shows real cross county variation, and non routine cognitive is the largest at roughly 0.34 of the four group total. @fig-dists shows both.

```{python}
#| label: fig-dists
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Distributions across the 12,087 county year panel. Purchasing power is right skewed with a long upper tail; the four task groups each show real cross county spread, with non routine cognitive the largest group."

share_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share",
            "non_routine_cognitive_share","non_routine_manual_share"]

titles=["Routine cognitive","Routine manual","Non routine cognitive","Non routine manual"]

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(16,3))
sns.histplot(data=df, x="affordability_salary", bins=50, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].set_title("Purchasing power ($)")
axes[0].set_xlabel("")
for i, (col, title) in enumerate(zip(share_cols, titles), start=1):
    sns.histplot(data=df, x=col, bins=50, color="#009E73", ax=axes[i])
    axes[i].set_title(title)
    axes[i].set_xlabel("")
    axes[i].set_ylabel("")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## Collinearity and the reference group

The four task group values described in @eq-group sum to one, so all four cannot enter a regression together. One serves as the reference, and we use non routine cognitive. Each remaining coefficient reads as the change in purchasing power associated with a shift out of non routine cognitive work and into that group, holding the controls fixed. No coefficient stands alone; every one is a comparison against the reference. The group values sit on a zero to one scale, so per percentage point figures divide the estimated coefficients by 100.

Normalizing also resolves a collinearity problem that would otherwise make these coefficients unusable. A variance inflation factor measures how much a coefficient is destabilized by its correlation with the other inputs, with a value above 10 the conventional threshold for concern. The unnormalized totals in @eq-weighted carry factors between 13 and 27, because all four are employment counts that scale together with county size, so they move together and carry little independent information. Dividing by the four group total removes that shared scale. @fig-vif shows the two specifications side by side: on the specification actually estimated, every factor sits between 1.2 and 1.6.

```{python}
#| label: fig-vif
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Variance inflation factors before and after normalization, drawn on a shared scale. The four unnormalized employment totals all sit above the threshold of 10 because they scale together with county size. Expressing them as proportions of the four group total removes that shared scale and leaves every factor near one."

raw=pd.read_sql("""
    select routine_cognitive, routine_manual, non_routine_cognitive, non_routine_manual
    from county_task_exposure
    """, engine)

raw_cols=["routine_cognitive","routine_manual","non_routine_cognitive","non_routine_manual"]
X_raw=sm.add_constant(raw[raw_cols])
vif_raw=pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(X_raw.values, i) for i in range(1, X_raw.shape[1])],
                  index=raw_cols)

X_vif=sm.add_constant(reg[reg_cols])
vif_share=pd.Series([variance_inflation_factor(X_vif.values, i) for i in range(1, X_vif.shape[1])],
                    index=reg_cols)

raw_labels=["Routine cognitive","Routine manual","Non routine cognitive","Non routine manual"]
share_labels=["Routine cognitive","Routine manual","Non routine manual"]
share_vals=vif_share[["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share",
                      "non_routine_manual_share"]].values
xmax=max(vif_raw.max(), 12)*1.08

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13,4))

axes[0].barh(raw_labels, vif_raw.values, color="#D55E00")
axes[0].axvline(10, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_xlim(0, xmax)
axes[0].set_title("Unnormalized employment totals")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Variance inflation factor")
for i, v in enumerate(vif_raw.values):
    axes[0].text(v+0.4, i, f"{v:.1f}", va="center", fontsize=10)

axes[1].barh(share_labels, share_vals, color="#009E73")
axes[1].axvline(10, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
axes[1].set_xlim(0, xmax)
axes[1].set_title("Group proportions, as estimated")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Variance inflation factor")
for i, v in enumerate(share_vals):
    axes[1].text(v+0.4, i, f"{v:.1f}", va="center", fontsize=10)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This is also the explanation for a problem visible earlier in the project. Before normalization the coefficients were unstable and their standard errors were large relative to their magnitudes, both standard symptoms of multicollinearity.

## Panel regression

Year indicators absorb conditions common to all counties within a year. These include the 2008 recession, the recovery through the 2010s, and the price movement that purchasing power does not itself deflate. Standard errors are clustered by county, since repeated observations of the same county across fifteen years are not independent draws. A Durbin Watson statistic of 0.496 confirms that dependence directly.

## Specification diagnostics

A linear model assumes the association holds at a constant rate across the range of the data, and that errors scatter symmetrically and evenly around the fit. We check both with residuals plotted against fitted values and a quantile quantile plot of the residuals. @fig-resid-analysis shows the two together and locates the failure directly.

Neither assumption holds. The smoothed residual line curves rather than tracking zero, and the vertical spread widens with fitted values. The model underpredicts both the least and the most affordable counties while fitting the middle well. The QQ plot bends away from the diagonal in the upper tail, which is the graphical form of a residual skew of 1.01.

```{python}
#| label: fig-resid-analysis
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Level model diagnostics. Left: residuals against fitted values with lowess smoother; the curve away from zero at both ends shows the model underpredicting the least and most affordable counties. Right: QQ plot of residuals; the bend above the line in the upper tail reflects the residual skew of 1.01."

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13,5))

sns.scatterplot(data=reg, x="fitted", y="resid", alpha=0.1, s=5, color="grey", ax=axes[0])
sns.regplot(data=reg, x="fitted", y="resid", scatter=False, lowess=True,
            line_kws={"color":"#D55E00"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Residuals against fitted values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted purchasing power ($)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual ($)")

stats.probplot(reg["resid"], dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

This failure is a result rather than a discarded attempt. The level model still delivers the interpretable estimates we report, and its own diagnostics establish that the data hold structure a straight line in dollars cannot represent.

## Log respecification

Underprediction at both extremes is the signature of a multiplicative process fit on an additive scale. The drivers of purchasing power act proportionally, so the same shift in an input moves a high purchasing power county by more dollars than a low one. Logging the outcome converts proportional effects into the additive form a linear model assumes.

Refitting the same specification on log purchasing power resolves most of the failure, as @fig-log-diag shows. Residual skew falls from 1.01 to 0.09. The spread becomes close to constant across the fitted range. The QQ plot tracks the diagonal through most of its range, departing only at the extreme tails.

```{python}
#| label: fig-log-diag
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Log model diagnostics, same layout as the level model. Residual skew falls from 1.01 to 0.09, the smoother lies close to zero, the spread is near constant, and the QQ plot tracks the diagonal through most of its range."

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13,5))

sns.scatterplot(data=reg, x="fitted_log", y="resid_log", alpha=0.1, s=5, color="grey", ax=axes[0])
sns.regplot(data=reg, x="fitted_log", y="resid_log", scatter=False, lowess=True,
            line_kws={"color":"#009E73"}, ax=axes[0])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Residuals against fitted values")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted log purchasing power")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Residual")

stats.probplot(reg["resid_log"], dist="norm", plot=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title("QQ plot")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@fig-binned puts the same comparison in the units of the outcome. Fitted values are cut into twenty equal count bins, and each point compares a bin's mean prediction with its mean actual value, so points on the line indicate no systematic bias in that range. On the level scale the model tracks purchasing power closely through the middle of the distribution, where most counties sit, but the least affordable bin comes in roughly \$8,000 above its prediction and the most affordable roughly \$9,000 above. On the log scale the points track the line throughout.

```{python}
#| label: fig-binned
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Binned means before and after the log transformation. Fitted values are cut into twenty equal count bins, and each point compares a bin's mean prediction with its mean actual value; points on the line indicate no systematic bias in that range. On the level scale both tails sit above the line. On the log scale the points track it throughout."

fig, axes=plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13,5.5))

reg.loc[:, "bin"]=pd.qcut(reg["fitted"], 20, labels=False)
binned=reg.groupby("bin")[["fitted","affordability_salary"]].mean()
axes[0].scatter(reg["fitted"], reg["affordability_salary"], alpha=0.05, s=4, color="grey")
axes[0].scatter(binned["fitted"], binned["affordability_salary"], color="#D55E00", zorder=3, s=35)
lim=[binned.values.min(), binned.values.max()]
axes[0].plot(lim, lim, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[0].set_title("Level target")
axes[0].set_xlabel("Fitted purchasing power ($)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Actual purchasing power ($)")

reg.loc[:, "bin_log"]=pd.qcut(reg["fitted_log"], 20, labels=False)
binned_log=reg.groupby("bin_log")[["fitted_log","actual_log"]].mean()
axes[1].scatter(reg["fitted_log"], reg["actual_log"], alpha=0.05, s=4, color="grey")
axes[1].scatter(binned_log["fitted_log"], binned_log["actual_log"], color="#009E73", zorder=3, s=35)
lim=[binned_log.values.min(), binned_log.values.max()]
axes[1].plot(lim, lim, color="black", linewidth=1)
axes[1].set_title("Log target")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Fitted log purchasing power")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Actual log purchasing power")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The smoothed line in @fig-log-diag still does not lie perfectly flat. The departures that remain are structure a single global transformation cannot absorb, most plausibly interactions among the inputs. That remaining curvature is the only reason to consider a more flexible model, and it is what the machine learning subsection tests.

## Variance decomposition

Purchasing power and the task groups vary both across counties and within a county over time, and the two carry different implications. @fig-between-within splits each group's variation into the two components. The manual groups vary almost entirely between counties, at roughly 10 and 25 percent within, which is what makes the associated differences durable rather than transient. Routine cognitive is the one group with genuine within county movement, near half its variance.

```{python}
#| label: fig-between-within
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Variation split into differences between counties and movement within a county over time, on the panel restricted to 2010 onward with each year's cross county mean removed. The manual groups vary almost entirely between counties. Routine cognitive is the one group with substantial within county movement."

df10=df[df["year"]>=2010].copy()
input_cols=["routine_cognitive_share","routine_manual_share","non_routine_manual_share"]

within_vals=[]
for col in input_cols:
    yd=df10[col]-df10.groupby("year")[col].transform("mean")
    within=(yd-yd.groupby(df10["county_fips"]).transform("mean")).var()
    within_vals.append(within/yd.var()*100)

labels=["Routine cognitive","Routine manual","Non routine manual"]
between_vals=[100-v for v in within_vals]

fig, ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(9,3.5))
ax.barh(labels, between_vals, color="#0072B2", label="Between counties")
ax.barh(labels, within_vals, left=between_vals, color="#D55E00",
        label="Within counties over time")
for i, v in enumerate(within_vals):
    ax.text(100-v/2, i, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", va="center", color="white", fontsize=10)
ax.set_xlim(0, 100)
ax.set_xlabel("Share of variance (percent)")
ax.legend(loc="lower center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.5), ncol=2, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The Census occupation coding change between 2009 and 2010, described in @sec-data, inflates apparent within county variation for the routine cognitive group. This is a feature of how the source data were coded rather than a property of the counties, so the figure above is computed on the panel restricted to 2010 onward with each year's cross county mean removed. We also repeat the main estimates on pre pandemic (2010 to 2019) and post pandemic (2021 to 2023) windows. Coefficient stability across these windows is reported in @sec-results.

## Machine learning models

The diagnostics above leave one open question: whether the residual curvature the log transformation cannot absorb represents real structure a more flexible model could capture. Following the model complexity ordering, we test the next two steps up from a linear specification, an ensemble of decision trees and a neural network.

All three models are fit on a split grouped by county, so every test prediction comes from a county the model has seen no rows of. This matters because a county's task composition barely moves from one year to the next, so its adjacent years are near duplicates; a random split would let a model recall a county rather than learn a relationship. The linear baseline is refit on the same rows and scored on the same held out counties, so the three are measured alike. Because these models are evaluated out of sample, their fit statistics are not comparable to the in sample figure from the panel regression above.

The random forest is tuned by grid search over tree count, depth, leaf size, and features considered per split, using grouped cross validation within the training counties. The neural network is kept deliberately shallow and narrow, with dropout and weight regularization added after an initial fit showed validation loss rising while training loss continued to fall. Both are fit on the logged outcome, so the comparison isolates flexibility rather than scale.

Feature importance is measured by shuffling each input in the held out data and recording the resulting drop in fit. This is preferred to importance computed during training, which tends to favor inputs offering more distinct split points. The four task groups are also shuffled jointly, since they are parts of a whole and their individual contributions are not additive. Two ablations complete the picture: refitting without the task groups, and refitting with the task groups alone.

## Summary

The analysis proceeds in one direction. The distributions show a skewed outcome. The variance inflation factors show why the task groups must enter as proportions with one omitted. The linear model on that specification yields an interpretable coefficient, and its own diagnostics show it is fit on the wrong scale. The log transformation corrects the scale and resolves most of the failure. What survives that correction is the question the flexible models are brought in to answer, and @sec-results reports what they found.
